---
title: "Conclusions"
---

This study has two limitations. First, there is a lack of information regarding the type of educational institution from which the respondents come. This information could have helped us refine our analysis of which types of people might be more or less willing to legitimize market-based criteria in education. Second, the scope of the study. To date, the multidimensional framework of meritocracy and privilege has been applied only in Chile, demonstrating that it can bring new perspectives to this research agenda. With this in mind, it is hoped that future studies will apply this multidimensional framework to new populations or even in cross-national comparative studies, thereby highlighting the role of beliefs about privilege in the study of market justice and opening the door to examining the contextual characteristics that may shape these relationships.

In addition to the future studies that may be undertaken, this paper seeks to contribute to the debate on educational justice within the context of a consolidated education market. By this, I mean revisiting concerns about the potential consequences of the commodification of education: normalizing market dynamics in a societal sphere such as education, without implementing the necessary safeguards for regulated operation, may end up further perpetuating existing inequalities. Although various policies have been implemented in Chile to address educational challenges such as discrimination and segregation (*Ley General de Enseñanza*, *Ley de Inclusión Escolar*, *Gratuidad universitaria*, for instance), it is necessary to establish forums that broaden the scope of the discussion and question the architecture of the Chilean educational system, along with the implications it has had and could have across various dimensions—namely, political, economic, and cultural. One element that can contribute to repositioning education in the national debate is understanding it as a matter of public concern. As Schinkel argues in the book of @camphuijsen_publicprivate_2026, beyond being a public good, education must be understood as a concern at both the governmental and societal levels. His arguments call for treating education as a shared concern, given that there is a universal desire for everyone to receive a good education. In this vein, education constitutes a shared societal project, one that has the potential to shape individuals and mold the character of a society. Therefore, education should not be merely a collection of private interests; rather, it is urgent to restore its public character in alignment with the common good.
